Amar Mujkicplasmid_analyis · notebooks_my/press → or space to advance · N for notes

Frame the talk in one line: we have measured the unnamed half of the small plasmidome, split it into artifact and residue, killed one hypothesis about what it is for, and pulled out one concrete object worth wet-lab time. Ask for interruptions — the methodological slides are where I most want pushback.

Openthe question

Half of the small-plasmid coding capacity has no name. That fact is compatible with two opposite worlds.

World A — idiosyncratic junk

Nearly every dark ORF unique. Non-adaptive sequence riding along on a selfish replicon. Nothing to find; the right response is to stop looking.

Prediction: almost every dark ORF is its own family.

World B — an annotation gap

A bounded set of uncharacterised protein families appearing over and over. Real biology that our tools have no name for. The right response is to fold them and test them.

Prediction: dark ORFs cluster into recurrent, lineage-crossing families.

These make opposite predictions about the shape of the dark proteome, so they can be separated by clustering the dark proteome against itself. That is where this project starts — and the answer turns out to be both, in measurable proportions.

upstream notebooks_my/cryptic_plasmids.ipynbthis argument notebooks_my/dark_plasmidome.ipynb

This is the whole talk in one slide. The two worlds are not a rhetorical device — they make different quantitative predictions, and the rest of the deck is a sequence of tests that discriminate between them. Emphasise that the honest answer is a partition, not a winner.

Part 1 · The resourceprovenance

Where 208,248 complete plasmids come from — and the skew that shapes everything after

Inclusion funneln
PlasmidScope ALL, deduplicated at 100% id / 100% cov852,600
complete / closed only208,360
− lab-made / synthetic−112
Working set208,248

Because the source is pre-deduplicated…

…there are no duplicate plasmids across source databases. Membership is overlapping and there are 102 distinct source combinations: IMG-PR 136,318 · RefSeq 56,042 · GenBank 55,428 · PLSDB 47,215 · COMPASS 12,084 · mMGE 7,207 · DDBJ 4,331 · ENA 4,049.

The skew to hold on to

129,680 plasmids (62%) are IMG-PR only — metagenome-assembled, usually with no isolate host and no curated metadata. The next-largest block, GenBank+PLSDB+RefSeq, is 23,998 well-curated isolate plasmids. Those two populations behave differently in every analysis that follows.

build scripts/characterize_plasmidscope_all.py → scripts/assemble_working_set.pynotebook notebooks_my/analysis.ipynb cell 2

The completeness gate is the expensive decision: it drops 644,240 entries. Defensible for a metadata study — you cannot type or annotate a fragment reliably — but I flag it again at the end as a real limitation for a family survey. The IMG-PR dominance is why so many later plasmids have no named host at all.

Part 1 · The resourcethe layers

Seven layers, folded into one 67-column table

1 · Physical

Size, GC, topology, source membership, straight from the assembled working set.

2 · Environment

A raw sampling label recovered for 85.9% from GOLD, NCBI BioSample and SRA, reconciled into a locked habitat taxonomy.

3 · Geography

Country for 76.5% of the analysis base (109,712 plasmids, 430 country/territory labels); 89,566 of those resolve to a point rather than a country centroid. Collection date for 62.9%.

4 · PLSDB curated

The 45,743 plasmids with a PLSDB record gain Inc typing, relaxase, MOB cluster, ecosystem and disease tags, species and AMRFinderPlus genes.

5 · Function

PlasAnn on 99.97% — CDS counts, replicons, oriV/oriT, and per-category gene counts (AMR, metal/biocide, conjugation, mobile element, toxin–antitoxin, virulence).

6 · Typing & mobility

mob_typer on 100%: mobility class, MOB family, 7,054 MOB primary clusters, predicted host range, and mob_rep_types — the replicon column this project uses.

7 · AMR

CARD v4.0.1 / RGI 6.0.8 over 595 shards, Perfect+Strict only. 14.1% AMR+, validated at 90.5% presence/absence concordance against PLSDB / AMRFinderPlus.

The join discipline

Everything downstream reads plasmid_metadata_master.tsv — 67 columns × 208,248 rows. Nothing in this talk re-derives a plasmid's metadata on the fly.

A standing rule

Replicon typing uses mob_rep_types only. No PlasmidFinder columns, no PlasAnn replicons, not even as a cross-check. Two slides on why.

build scripts/build_metadata_master.py · recover_env_local.py · fetch_biosample_env.py · scrape_img_geo.py · enrich_plsdb_metadata.py · harvest_plasann.py · harvest_typing.py · harvest_card.py

Do not read the cards out. The two things worth saying aloud: every layer is a separate script writing a separate TSV that one builder folds in, so any number here is traceable to one file; and the coverage numbers are wildly uneven across layers — 100% for mobility, 46% for host, 22% for PLSDB curation. Uneven coverage is a recurring source of fake signal in this project.

Part 1 · The resourcehosts

Who carries them — and why host is metadata, not a clean variable

Coverage

A host is populated for 96,230 / 208,248 (46.2%) — 6,778 species across 1,365 genera. The other 54% are mostly IMG-PR metagenomic plasmids with no isolate at all.

Skew

E. coli 14,460 and K. pneumoniae 10,477 alone are a quarter of all hosted plasmids. The host column is Enterobacterales-skewed by construction — it reflects clinical surveillance effort, not plasmid biology.

Why it matters later

62,357 plasmids carry both a host genus and a country. When host genus enters the AMR model in Part 3, it takes about half of the One Health compartment effect with it.

notebook analysis.ipynb cells 5, 10, 12–13 — host joined from PlasmidScope via the provenance rep→full key bridge

Treat host as partial-coverage metadata, never as a clean column. The country panel is the one to point at: it is not showing you where plasmids are, it is showing you which countries run Enterobacterales surveillance. Every geographic contrast in this project has that confound underneath it.

Two tiers, and one column we refuse to use

Domain (Human / Animal / Environment / Plant & food) over the raw hab_sub label. hab_top is not an analysis variable — its only job was to draw the analysis set. One Health compartments are built from hab_sub + is_clinical, and the map is imported from the Phase-3 script so the notebook cannot drift from it.

The shape of the sampling

“Human: unspecified” alone is 22,793 plasmids — more than every animal habitat combined. Freshwater is 15,193. Air is 135, fungi 177. Any environmental contrast is drawn between wildly unequal n.

scripts recover_env_local.py · fetch_biosample_env.py · fetch_sra_env.py · reconcile_environment.pylocked taxonomy reports/environment_taxonomy_LOCKED.md

The simulated-communities exclusion is worth 20 seconds: 64,658 plasmids from GOLD's synthetic-community entries, which are a sampling artefact, not a habitat. We filter on hab_top, not geo_source — filtering on geo_source leaves nine of them in. It is a locked decision made before any analysis, and it is the single largest cut in the project.

Part 2 · Repliconsthe instrument

Replicon typing: mob_typer only, and the two reasons why

75,751
carry ≥1 replicon marker — 52.8% of the analysis base
1,759
distinct replicon types

1 · Coverage

mob_typer types roughly twice as many plasmids as PlasmidFinder does on this collection, and it types them evenly. It also supplies mob_cluster, the lineage proxy every clonal-redundancy control in this talk depends on.

2 · PlasmidFinder inflates multireplicon counts

Its Col entries overlap: 39.9% of PF-typed small plasmids match Col, ColRNAI and Col440I, and 82.6% of “multi-family” small plasmids have families that are all Col variants. Counting those as three replicons is not a finding.

The cost of the choice

mob_rep_types has no family-level rollup — it mixes named Inc types (IncFIB, IncFII) with bare rep_cluster_NNNN identifiers. Any family grouping has to be derived and stated. And 47% of the analysis base gets no replicon call at all.

typing scripts/mobtyper_array.sbatch → scripts/harvest_typing.py · reports/typing_methodology.mdnotebook analysis.ipynb cell 16

There is a third reason that only emerged at peer review, and it is the strongest — PlasmidFinder typing coverage varies nine-fold across One Health compartments, from 38.1% clinical to 4.3% natural environment. Any cross-compartment replicon comparison built on it compares groups whose reference category means different things. That is on the refutation slide.

Part 2 · Repliconsthe original question

The multireplicon question — what this project was designed around

18,685 plasmids carry ≥2 distinct replicon types — 24.7% of typed plasmids, 13.0% of the analysis base. Maximum on one replicon: 7.

It tracks the human–clinical axis

Human 30.9% · Animal 28.1% · Plant & food 17.0% · Environment 15.0%. At habitat level the top is respiratory 40.8%, blood 40.7%, cattle 37.1%; the bottom is bioreactor 4.0%.

Read it conditioned

Every rate here is per typed plasmid, which removes typing-coverage differences between groups — but it cannot remove what the untyped plasmids would have been. The comparison is between the typeable fractions, not between the habitats.

notebook analysis.ipynb cells 17, 19 — Fisher vs rest, BH-corrected, Wilson 95% CIs

This was the central biological question the whole resource was built to answer: how many plasmids carry two or more distinct replicons, and what distinguishes them. Note that the ordering — human-clinical high, environmental low — is the same ordering as AMR prevalence in Part 3. That is a hint that both are partly tracking something else, and Part 4 says what.

Part 2 · Repliconsstructure

Replicons co-occur non-randomly — and half the network has no name

How the edges are drawn

242 candidate replicons (≥50 occurrences) → 908 pairs → one-sided Fisher exact per pair, BH-corrected, keeping only q < 0.05, OR ≥ 2.0, ≥20 plasmids sharing the pair. Result: 121 edges over 77 nodes in 12 modules.

The IncF hub is real

IncFIB / IncFIC / IncFIA / IncFII sit in one dense core with IncU, IncR, IncQ1, IncN and IncHI2A hanging off it — the multireplicon architecture of the Enterobacterales resistance plasmid, recovered without being told to look for it.

And this is the door into Act II

Most of the network is grey. The grey nodes are rep_cluster_NNNN — replicon families mob_typer can distinguish but nobody has named. Whole modules of the co-occurrence structure carry no Inc label at all.

Add the 47% of plasmids that get no replicon call whatsoever, and the pattern is already visible at the level of the replicon vocabulary, one level up from where Act II works.

notebook analysis.ipynb cell 18 — networkx, greedy modularity communities

This is my favourite Act I figure and the cleanest bridge in the talk. The named part of the graph reproduces textbook plasmid biology. The unnamed part is bigger. If you accept that the replicon vocabulary is half-empty, the claim in Act II — that the protein vocabulary is half-empty too — stops sounding surprising.

Part 2 · Repliconsconsequences

What a second replicon buys — once you take plasmid size out of it

Resistance

56.4% of multireplicon plasmids are AMR+ vs 23.1% of single-replicon — raw OR 4.30. Size-and-GC-adjusted OR 2.42 (95% CI 2.33–2.52), with size itself at OR 3.41 per log₁₀ bp.

Host range

Multireplicon plasmids have broader predicted host range: mean breadth 3.41 vs 2.94 (Mann–Whitney p → 0). Prediction available for 64.7% of the base.

The named broad types check out

IncW, IncP, Inc11 and Inc13 sit at the multi-phyla end — the classic broad-host-range backbones — while many rep_cluster types are genus-restricted. The instrument recovers what it should.

notebook analysis.ipynb cells 20, 24–26 · host range = mob_typer predicted rank, genus → multi-phyla

The size adjustment is the point. Raw OR 4.3 is a headline; 2.4 is the finding. Roughly half of the raw association is that multireplicon plasmids are bigger and bigger plasmids carry more of everything. This is the first appearance of the confound that goes on to eat our manuscript thesis two slides from now. Also note host range is a mob_typer prediction, neighbourhood-based — not an observation.

run CARD v4.0.1 / RGI 6.0.8, Perfect+Strict only · scripts/card_array.sbatch → harvest_card.py → aggregate_card.pyreport reports/card_amr_methodology.md

Read the top of the gene list aloud: sul1, TEM-1, qacEdelta1, sul2, aadA. That is a class-1 integron cassette array, gene for gene — qacEdelta1 and sul1 are the 3′ conserved segment. The plasmid resistome as CARD sees it is dominated by one mobile genetic platform. Strict filtering is deliberate: we drop Loose hits entirely, which costs sensitivity and buys the 90.5% concordance.

Part 3 · AMRmobility & the clonal control

Mobility is a large effect — and clonal over-sampling halves everything

Mobility

conjugative 60.1% · mobilizable 18.9% · non-mobilizable 6.7%. The compartment gradient holds within every mobility class, and the mobility gradient holds within every compartment.

The clonal control

Re-run on one random plasmid per MOB cluster (6,182 of 7,054 clusters): clinical 44.6% → 23.8%, livestock 38.9% → 22.0%, wildlife 1.8% → 0.9%. Absolute prevalences roughly halve.

What survives

The ordering is preserved and clinical/livestock stay the top two. Read the raw percentages as an upper bound inflated by clonal over-sampling, the dereplicated ones as a lower bound, and the gradient as the robust finding.

report reports/amr_onehealth_methodology.md §3.3, §4 · MOB dereplication is the same control used throughout Act II

Point out that this is exactly the same control that later saves us in the dark-families work — one plasmid per MOB cluster. Different data, different question, same failure mode: clinical clones are massively over-sequenced, and any prevalence you compute over raw deposits inherits that. MOB clustering is coarse, 7,054 clusters for 208,248 plasmids, so it over-collapses; the truth sits between the two columns.

Part 3 · AMRrepertoires

Two loosely-coupled resistome blocks, and 171 genes that reach everywhere

The structure is two blocks

A human block (clinical ↔ community, Jaccard 0.53) and an agricultural–environmental block (livestock, plant & food, natural, engineered — 0.42–0.47 among themselves), with only 0.33–0.37 sharing between them. Least shared of all: clinical ↔ wildlife, 0.15.

But 17% of ARGs are everywhere

Of 982 distinct ARGs on AMR+ plasmids, 517 (53%) appear in one domain and 171 (17%) span all four. Unique-ARO richness: clinical 686 → wildlife 109.

Compartment signatures

Clinical: β-lactam 66%, carbapenem 33%. Livestock: aminoglycoside 59%, tetracycline 53% — the veterinary classes. Engineered interface: disinfectants 44% — biocide co-selection. Plant & food: tetracycline 53%, fluoroquinolone 33%.

Read with the sampling in mind

Domains are unevenly sampled (Human 13,984 AMR+ vs Plant & food 891), so “seen in a domain” is easier for Human. The all-four-domain genes are the robust part — they surface despite the small denominators.

notebook analysis.ipynb cell 27 · report reports/amr_onehealth_methodology.md §3.5–§3.6

The compartment signatures are the most satisfying result in Act I because nothing was tuned to produce them: growth-promoter classes in livestock, biocides in wastewater, carbapenems in the clinic. That is external validity for the whole compartment map — the taxonomy was locked before we looked, and it recovers the classes each setting is known to use.

Part 3 · AMRpeer review

We wrote it up for NAR. The reviewers were right, and the central claim did not survive.

The title claim was a size artefact

We argued “mobility rivals provenance” from a raw contrast: environmental conjugative plasmids at 27.4% vs clinical non-mobilizable at 23.9%. Those cells differ 3.4-fold in median length — 99,516 bp vs 29,120 bp. At matched size the clinical non-mobilizable plasmid is the likelier carrier at every point tested: 7.4% vs 4.1% at 5 kb, 38.8% vs 25.3% at 100 kb. The sentence the paper was named after reversed.

Half the compartment effect is host lineage

Adding host genus attenuates every major effect by close to half — clinical OR 7.66 → 3.30, community 6.03 → 3.15, livestock 5.22 → 2.85. Pseudo-R² rises 0.243 → 0.299. “Nine times likelier” becomes about three.

And three more

  • Precision overstated 2–9×: with SEs clustered on MOB cluster every CI widens, and the GC effect vanishes entirely (p = 0.31).
  • 61% of the raw conjugative effect is plasmid size — OR 12.23 without log_size, 4.77 with it.
  • The multireplicon section was cut: PlasmidFinder typing coverage varies nine-fold across the compartments being compared (38.1% clinical → 4.3% natural).

One objection we refuted

The 39,331 plasmids excluded for lacking a habitat label carry AMR at 17.86% against 18.81% in the analysed set. Habitat-label recovery is close to non-informative for resistance — which defuses the manuscript's own “single largest threat” framing.

produced by scripts/reassess_review_findings.py → manuscript/reassessment_round1.md · 4 of 6 objections upheld, 1 upheld with qualification, 1 refuted

State the honest qualification on the host adjustment: host coverage is 99.2% for clinical and 20.1% for wildlife, so the host-adjusted model runs on a subset that over-represents exactly the compartments with the strongest effects. The before/after is internally valid — same rows, both models — but generalising the ~50% attenuation assumes a representativeness the data do not establish. The defensible thesis now: apparent One Health structure in plasmid resistomes is substantially explained by host lineage and plasmid size and roughly halves when either is controlled — but a real compartment gradient and a real mobility effect both survive. That is more conservative and, because it quantifies how much of an assumed pattern is compositional, arguably more useful.

Part 4 · The bridgewhat Act I taught us

Three lessons, and the one that sent us into the dark

1 · Size eats everything

It reversed the mobility claim. It halved the multireplicon–AMR odds ratio, 4.30 → 2.42. It is the dominant single predictor in every model we fitted.

Carries into Act II: defense-system carriage rises 24× across CDS bands, and we report it stratified rather than as a rate.

2 · Composition beats biology unless controlled

Host lineage took half the compartment effect. MOB dereplication halved every prevalence. Country contrasts turn out to measure who runs surveillance.

Carries into Act II: the same MOB-cluster control decides whether a recurrent dark family is real or one clone sequenced eight hundred times.

3 · Half the vocabulary is already unnamed

47% of plasmids get no replicon call at all. Of those that do, whole modules of the co-occurrence network are rep_cluster_NNNN with no Inc name. And the plasmids that go untyped are small.

This is the door. We had built a 208,248-plasmid resource and the tools were silent on the modal plasmid in it.

We went looking for the plasmids our own instrument could not see — and found that half the small plasmidome carries no payload, no name, and no annotation at all.

Act I analysis.ipynb · amr_onehealth_methodology.md · reassessment_round1.mdAct II starts here notebooks_my/cryptic_plasmids.ipynb

This is the hinge of the talk — take your time. The three lessons are not filler; each one reappears as a named control in Act II, and I want the room to recognise them when they do. Then hand over to the second act with the last line.

“Payload-free” means

  • no CARD/RGI resistance gene (card_n_arg = 0)
  • no PlasAnn virulence gene
  • no PlasAnn metal / biocide resistance gene

Conjugation machinery is not disqualifying here. Neither, as it turns out, are defense systems — see Part 4.

Physical profile of the 71,414

Median 4,758 bp (IQR 3,308–7,178) · median 6 CDS · GC 44.9%.
Mobility: 49,908 non-mobilizable · 21,330 mobilizable · 176 conjugative.
Replicon call from mob_typer on only 35.0%; 65% are untypeable.

This is not a niche subset. It is the modal plasmid in a complete-genome database, and it is the part of the plasmidome that plasmid biology has the least to say about.

notebook notebooks_my/cryptic_plasmids.ipynb cells 0–2, 15, 17report reports/small_cryptic_methodology.md

The 65% replicon no-call rate is worth pausing on — it means the standard typing toolkit is already blind to two thirds of this set before we even get to the proteins. If asked why 20 kb: it is the size threshold in the locked small-cryptic methodology, and the size distribution is genuinely bimodal around it.

The named half is pure backbone

The coverage setting is stricter than anything comparable in the literature. The identity threshold is not, and Part 6 is about exactly how much rests on it. Lineage proxy throughout: mob_cluster, the MOB-suite primary cluster — 4,004 of them in this subset.

scripts extract_plasann_proteins.py → cluster_dark_orfs.sh → summarize_dark_orf_clusters.pyreport reports/dark_orf_clustering.md

Flag the deliberate asymmetry: we were stricter than the field on coverage and at the loose end on identity. Both choices are defensible individually; together they produce the non-nesting problem that bites us in Part 7. The dark proteome is recurrent, not idiosyncratic

Recurrent

84.7%
of dark ORFs sit in a family with at least one other member.

Idiosyncratic

15.3%
singletons — 57,935 families of one. World A is not what the data look like.

notebook dark_plasmidome.ipynb §1 (R1)table data/dark_orf_run/darkfam_stats.tsv

This is the first real result and it is unambiguous: the junk reading is not supported. But say immediately that recurrence on its own proves nothing — the same lineage sequenced a thousand times produces exactly this picture. That is the next slide, and it is the trap that has caught us before in this project.

Part 6 · Recurrenceresult 2 — the control

Recurrence survives the clonal-redundancy control

241,727 dark ORFs — 63.9% of the dark proteome — sit in families spanning ≥2 independent MOB lineages. Among substantial families (≥10 members), 79.2% cross lineage boundaries, median 4 lineages and 5 habitats.

Why this control exists

A genus-level Acinetobacter signal earlier in this project collapsed to two MOB clusters once dereplicated. Every prevalence claim in this deck is reported against lineage spread for that reason.

notebook dark_plasmidome.ipynb §2 (R2)lineage proxy mob_cluster from scripts/harvest_typing.py — 4,004 clusters in the subset

Panel B is the one to talk to: the dashed line is the ceiling (one lineage per protein). The mass sits well below it but climbs with family size, which is what you expect from genuinely mobile proteins and not what a single expanded clone would produce. Caveat honestly: the subset is lineage-skewed — cluster AA379 alone holds 19,427 of the 71,414 plasmids.

Part 6 · Recurrenceresult 3

86% have no named homolog anywhere in the annotated set

Co-clustering rules out the cheapest explanation — that PlasAnn can name these proteins and simply failed on these particular plasmids. Only 14.1% of dark ORFs land in a family holding a named member. 5,028 dark-only families have ≥10 members, holding almost half of all dark protein content.

But this is still PlasAnn compared against itself. “No named homolog” is not yet evidence of novelty — it only means one tool is silent in two different ways. The next test brings in an external database, and it takes a large bite out of this number.

notebook dark_plasmidome.ipynb §3 (R3) · mix30 co-clustering

Deliberately undercut our own headline here. When we wrote “85.9% have no named homolog” we were, at that moment, over-claiming — and the Pfam run is what showed it. Setting that up now makes the Part 3 result land as rigour rather than as a retraction.

Part 7 · Artifact or realdesign

Pfam-A, with a positive control and a propagation check

DARKREP — the test

92,752
one representative per dark family.

NAMED — positive control

78,397
every protein PlasAnn did name. Without it, a low dark hit rate is ambiguous.

VALID — propagation check

3,678
all members of 200 sampled families — does a representative stand for its family?

The threshold is not ours

hmmsearch --cut_ga against Pfam-A 38.2 (30,134 families, 2026-01). Pfam's own curated per-family gathering thresholds — so no e-value is chosen by us and there is no knob to tune post hoc.

Compute

88-task SLURM array, 174,827 query sequences, 4 cores / 12 GB per task. Everything weighted by family size, so a hit on a 1,000-member family is not counted like a hit on a singleton.

scripts build_pfam_query.py → pfam_array.sbatch → summarize_pfam.py → pfam_verdict.pyreport reports/pfam_dark_validation.md

The positive control is the design decision I would defend hardest. A 26% dark hit rate means nothing on its own — plasmid proteins could simply be badly covered by Pfam. It only becomes evidence when the named set from the same plasmids, searched the same way, hits at 77%.

What Pfam rescued is the plasmid backbone, unlabelled

18.5% of the dark proteome

Rep_1, Rep3_N/C, Mob_Pre, NikA-like, Relaxase, MobA_MobL, RepL, ParE, RelB, YoeB, YafQ, TraD — proteins PlasAnn has categories for.

A Pfam hit is not a function

10.1% of the rescue is a Domain of Unknown Function — 2,914 families across 1,002 distinct DUFs. Named, still unexplained.

Propagation holds

Members agree with their family representative's Pfam status 96.1% of the time (200 families, 3,678 members); 23/200 families are internally mixed.

notebook dark_plasmidome.ipynb §5 (R5) — Pfam's own DE/TP/CL annotation, not our regexclans Pfam-A.clans.tsv.gz

Worth saying plainly: Section 1's finding that the dark proteome “looks like replicate-and-mobilise machinery” was right for a duller reason than novelty — some of it literally is that machinery, unlabelled. Also note the clan panel: 17.4% of rescued ORFs are in families Pfam assigns to no clan at all, which is its own kind of frontier.

Part 7 · Artifact or realwhat survives

The claim that survives is narrower and better supported

A large, lineage-spanning protein space in the small plasmidome is invisible to both plasmid-specific annotation and Pfam.

What we withdrew

“85.9% of dark ORFs have no named homolog” stands as computed but is no longer evidence of novelty — a third of that 85.9% is recognisable to Pfam.

What Pfam does not settle

No hit at --cut_ga is not proof of structural novelty. Profile HMMs run out well before structure does. That is the next experiment, not a caveat.

candidate list data/pfam_run/dark_novel_families.tsv (3,343 rows)report reports/pfam_dark_validation.md §4.4

This is the honest headline of Parts 2–3 and the number I would put in an abstract: 115,811 dark ORFs in 3,343 recurrent, lineage-crossing families that neither tool can name. Everything after this is about narrowing that to something you can actually do an experiment on.

Part 7 · Artifact or realerrata

Two defects found and fixed mid-run — one of them mattered a lot

Defect 1 — duplicate protein records

Plasmids present in both PlasAnn shard series contributed their proteins twice.

0.22% of records

Cosmetic. Fixed by de-duplicating on plasmid ID before extraction.

Defect 2 — the CDS index broke the join

Dark ORFs are matched to the full-CDS FASTA by {plasmid}|{cds_index}. The index was computed over all features rather than over CDS only, so the key did not line up.

40,572 of 378,552 dark ORFs — 10.7%

Every one of them was silently miscounted as “no Pfam match”, i.e. as novel. Failing loudly would have been better than the answer we liked.

To be unambiguous about what “post-fix” means

Both fixes were applied to the pipeline in August, and the affected data files were rebuilt then. Every figure in this deck — before this slide and after it — was regenerated from the current data, so no slide anywhere shows a pre-fix number. The dark-ORF total is 378,552 throughout; it was 379,397 before the dedup, and recurrence moved 84.75% → 84.70%. No conclusion changed.

The join is now asserted in the notebook rather than assumed, and the per-plasmid dark count is computed by two independent routes — the PlasAnn TSV and the FASTA headers — which agree to 100.00% on all 63,993 carriers.

The audit that caught this is the same one that later produced the clustering-compliance result in Part 10. The failure mode to worry about in this kind of work is not a wrong answer — it is a join that quietly drops rows into the interesting bucket.

documented reports/pfam_dark_validation.md §6.1–§6.2 · reports/dark_orf_clustering.md “Corrections (2026-08-28)”cross-check cryptic_plasmids.ipynb cell 22

Do not rush past this. In a room of people who will re-run this kind of pipeline, showing the bug that inflated our own novelty estimate by ten percentage points buys more credibility than any result on the deck. It also motivates the two independent counting routes we now run for every headline quantity.

Part 8 · What is it forhypothesis

Hypothesis: the dark plasmidome is anti-defense

Why it is a good hypothesis

  • Anti-CRISPR proteins are 50–150 aa, hyperdiverse, and share no common fold — precisely the profile of an unannotatable ORF.
  • Plasmids have every reason to carry them.
  • psiA/psiB (anti-SOS) and ardA/klcA/ocr (anti-restriction) are classic conjugative-plasmid cargo.
  • Our dark median is 138 aa. It fits.

Pfam is the wrong instrument

Pfam holds ~11 anti-CRISPR models against >100 experimentally characterised Acr families.

So: dbAPIS — 290 HMMs = 200 anti-prokaryotic-immune-system families + 90 anti-CRISPR families. Roughly 8× Pfam's Acr coverage.

Two complications, handled explicitly rather than hidden ↓

1. No curated thresholds

dbAPIS models carry no GA/TC/NC lines, unlike Pfam. A cutoff has to be chosen — so results are reported at three stringency tiers and the conclusion must not depend on which you pick.

2. Cross-hits to housekeeping

Several dbAPIS models fire on abundant plasmid proteins. Every hit is adjudicated against its independent Pfam assignment instead of being taken at face value.

notebook notebooks_my/antidefense.ipynb §1–§3search scripts/dbapis_search.sbatch

Present this as a hypothesis we wanted to be true. It is the most attractive functional story available for a hyperdiverse short-ORF population, and if it had held it would have been the paper. Setting it up sincerely is what makes the rejection worth a slide.

Part 8 · What is it forrejected

No. And the raw database output was inflated threefold.

Adjudication of the 106 standard-tier hits

65.7% are contradicted by Pfam. The single largest “anti-CRISPR” signal — AcrIIA21, 68 ORFs — is RepA_N, a replication initiator.

Reported uncritically, this analysis would have called plasmid replication proteins anti-CRISPRs.

460
dark ORFs at face value (0.122%)
158
after adjudication — 0.042% of the dark proteome
  • Stringency tiers give 0.167% / 0.122% / 0.102% — the answer does not depend on the cutoff.
  • Anti-CRISPR specifically: 9 families, 63 ORFs — 0.017%.
  • Independent third screen (DefenseFinder --antidefensefinder) reproduces the same two false positives and lands at 91 ORFs, 0.024%.
notebook antidefense.ipynb §3–§6limit rules out known anti-defense families — dbAPIS holds 90 Acr families; the true number is larger

Two things to keep even though the hypothesis died. First, the adjudication rule is deliberately aggressive — it discards any hit whose Pfam call is plasmid housekeeping, which will also discard genuine anti-defense proteins carrying an HTH or Rep-like domain, so 158 is a floor, not an estimate. Second: classic anti-defense genes are not hiding in the dark at all — psiA/psiB appear 69 times in the named proteome and about 15 times in the dark one. Where plasmids carry them, existing tools already find them.

Part 8 · What is it forthe surprise

The unexpected result is on the defense side — our payload definition has a hole in it

3,647 defense systems on 3,362 of 65,805 plasmids (5.1%) that our definition calls empty. Restriction–modification is 44% of everything found, plus MazEF, HEC-09, AbiQ, Thoeris, Kiwa, CBASS, Retron.

Payload-free never excluded defense

The definition was: no AMR, no virulence, no metal/biocide. A plasmid carrying a complete Type II RM system is still “payload-free” under it. That is a gap in the definition, and it needs a sentence in any write-up that uses the term.

A different evidence rule

DefenseFinder 3.0.0 was run on whole plasmids in gene order (MacSyFinder gembase), so it uses genomic context to call a system. Every other screen in this project is pure homology.

notebook notebooks_my/defense_systems.ipynbinput scripts/build_defensefinder_input.py · 65,805 plasmids / 456,949 proteins, 33-task array

Caveat on the same slide: 43.9% of Defense calls rest on a single gene. For RM_Type_IIG, AbiQ, HEC-09 and PD-T4-5 that is the correct architecture, not weak evidence; for others it means the system is incomplete. The context-supported subset is 2,045 systems on 1,956 plasmids — 2.97%.

Part 8 · What is it forconfounds

Defense carriage is size-confounded, but it is not clonal

The size confound governs everything

Carriage rises 0.69% → 16.68% across CDS bands — a 24× gradient. A defense system needs genes to be detected, so “5.1% of plasmids carry one” is substantially a statement about plasmid size.

Stratified, not corrected. Every prevalence number is conditional on this.

The clonal control passes — backwards

Carriers span 858 MOB lineages. Carriage falls as lineages grow: 10.5% in singleton lineages → 3.0% in lineages of >100.

The mega-lineages that dominate this subset are defense-poor — the opposite of what clonal inflation produces.

Ecology: real, but don't rank it

The One Health compartment effect survives CDS stratification in all four bands (χ² p < 1e-11), but the ranking is not stable across bands.

Safe claim: carriage varies by compartment. Unsafe claim: which compartment is highest.

An audit we did not run

The AntiDefenseFinder half of this same run produced verified false positives. No equivalent audit was run on the Defense side; the RM calls are multi-gene and better supported, but the single-gene types were not independently checked against Pfam. That is an open task, not a solved one.

Coverage

12,077 of 65,805 plasmids have no One Health compartment, so the ecology analysis covers 82% of the set. A further 5,569 payload-free plasmids have no PlasAnn genes at all and are absent from all of this.

notebook defense_systems.ipynb §2–§4compartments built from hab_sub + is_clinical, map imported from scripts/analyze_amr_onehealth_mobility.py

The falling-carriage-with-lineage-size result is genuinely nice and I would like opinions on it: is defense-poverty in the mega-lineages a real biological signal (successful lineages shed defense?), or is it a property of how mob_cluster assigns the big metagenomic groups? I do not know, and it would be a paper if it is the former.

Defense explains ~55× more of the dark proteome than anti-defense does, and it still barely registers. This is the slide that motivates going to structure rather than to more HMM databases.

Counted as families it looks idiosyncratic; counted as ORFs it does not

By family

63.0% of families sit on exactly one plasmid.

By ORF

Those one-offs are only 15.6% of the dark proteome. 84.4% of dark ORFs are in families found on two or more plasmids.

Both statements are true of the same table. The rest of this section follows the ORFs, because the question is how much coding capacity recurs, not how many rare families exist.

Small slide, important habit. Every “X% of the dark plasmidome” claim in the literature needs its unit stated, and switching unit here flips the qualitative reading from “mostly one-offs” to “mostly recurrent”.

Part 9 · Narrowinga warning

The commonest dark proteins are mostly badly annotated ones

17 of the 25 most prevalent dark families have a Pfam name, and the names are Rep_1, Rep3_C, Replicase, Mob_Pre, NikA-like, RelB, YoeB, YafQ, wHTH_Par, TraD, Resolvase — the plasmid backbone. Those are annotation failures, not discoveries.

The gradient is systematic

Pfam names 24% of families seen on one plasmid, and 66% of those seen on 500+. Prevalence and darkness pull apart, monotonically.

notebook dark_families.ipynb §3–§4

This is the slide that stops anyone building a shortlist by prevalence alone — which is the obvious first thing to do and the wrong thing to do. Panel B is the second half of the warning: a family on 800 plasmids but only 3–9 MOB clusters is one lineage sequenced repeatedly, not a widely distributed protein.

Part 10 · Thresholdsthe audit

MMseqs2 was not enforcing the criterion our methods claimed

MMseqs2's own help states that cascaded clustering “can cluster sequences that do not fulfil the clustering criteria”, corrected by --cluster-reassign. We had not passed it. The audit aligns every sampled member back to its own representative — no transitive links.

clusteringpairscompliantfails cov
30%, as published (no reassign)1,06689.12%111
30% + --cluster-reassign1,61999.26%11
50% + reassign94499.58%1
70% + reassign1,28699.92%0
90% + reassign719100.00%0

Roughly one member in nine did not meet the criterion we documented — almost always on coverage. Adding the flag at the same identity yields +7.1% families and moves 12.0% of members to a different family.

This does not put homology in doubt — the worst member-to-representative E-value in the largest family was 1.2e-43. The enforced criterion was simply looser than the stated one.

So: sweep, don't pick

Rebuilt at four identity thresholds, reassignment on, coverage held at 80% both ways. The thresholds are literature landmarks: 50% = UniRef50, 70% = NMPFamsDB, 90% = UniRef90.

scripts recluster_dark_orfs.sh · recluster_sweep.sbatch · audit_cluster_compliance.py · recluster_pfam_array.sbatchreport reports/clustering_threshold_sensitivity.md

Nothing under the original dark30_* outputs was modified, so the earlier reports and notebooks stay reproducible — the sweep lives in its own directory. If anyone asks why we did not just re-run everything at 30%+reassign: because then the sensitivity result disappears into a single number, and the sensitivity is the result.

Five families survive every filter at UniRef90

Short proteins held at ≥90% amino-acid identity across 14–42 independent MOB lineages and up to 20 habitats, with no Pfam-A match at --cut_ga.

That combination is hard to explain by sampling. Clonal expansion produces high identity within one lineage, not across forty. Sequence conservation that strong across that many independent lineages is the signature of purifying selection — which means these proteins are doing something.

The cost of the conservative choice

93 families at 30% → 61 with the criterion enforced → 39 at UniRef50 → 19 at 70% → 5 here. 788 dark ORFs, 0.21% of the dark proteome.
Fewest candidates, strongest claim per candidate.

If the point is a shortlist for structure prediction and wet-lab work, these five are where the evidence is strongest per candidate.

Part 10 · Thresholdsthe confound, sharpened

Tightening identity does not remove the sampling confound — it sharpens it

The five most prevalent families at 90% overlap on 70–97% of their carriers. 477 plasmids carry all five — median 4,244 bp (IQR 4,225–4,247), 2 MOB clusters, 100% with no replicon call, 78% Human: unspecified.

That is one heavily sequenced Bacteroides cryptic plasmid, not five widespread protein families.

The control

The sixth-ranked family shares no carriers with those five and sits on a ~2,857 bp replicon — which is what shows the overlap is real and family-specific rather than an artefact of how we measured it.

Why it gets worse, not better: near-identical clustering tracks clonal expansion almost exactly. Lineage spread, not plasmid count, is what separates biology from sequencing effort — at every threshold.

notebook dark_families_90pct.ipynb §3

This is the counter-intuitive one and worth slowing down for. The instinct is that a stricter identity threshold gives you a “cleaner” answer. It gives you a cleaner definition of a family and a dirtier prevalence statistic, because what it now measures is how often that exact plasmid was deposited.

The general lesson: of the 20 most lineage-spread dark ORFs, nine sit in Pfam-named families, and the names are PhdYeFM_antitox, ParE_toxin, YafQ_toxin, MazE_antitoxin, RelB, HTH_Tnp_1 — toxin–antitoxin systems and transposases. Part 12 · The cassettetwo candidates

Two families, picked for being ecologically wide on very few lineages

representativeaaplasmidslineageshabitatsPfam
ORF-AGenBank_CP063716.1|6155400523none
ORF-BIMGPR_plasmid_2609460067_000008|1132355521none

Both unannotatable by PlasAnn, no Pfam-A match at --cut_ga, and both at the 90% clustering — so “family” here means near-identical protein. They were the most habitat-spread entries in the 90% top 20 while sitting on a handful of lineages, which is an odd combination and the reason we looked.

They are one object, not two findings

336 plasmids carry both — 84% of ORF-A's carriers and 95% of ORF-B's, Jaccard 0.80. Every one of those 336 is mobilizable, median 5,192 bp.

A denominator that is easy to get wrong

Merging the two ORFs by plasmid gives 365 rows over 336 carriers, because 11 plasmids carry a duplicate copy and contribute several A–B pairings. Percentages must be taken per carrier: the offset statistic is 87% per carrier against 81% per pairing; the mobilisation-gene share 72% against 61%.

notebook notebooks_my/zoom_two_dark_orfs.ipynb §1clustering 90% id / 80% cov, --cluster-reassign 1

Note how we got here: not from the 93-family shortlist, but from the 90% top-20 by an odd ratio — many habitats, few lineages. Worth flagging as a search heuristic in its own right.

Part 12 · The cassettearchitecture

They flank the relaxase, at a fixed spacing, on a Col156 backbone

  • |offset| = 2 on 87% of the 336 carriers — never adjacent, always exactly one gene apart.
  • That gene is a mobilisation gene (moB or mobA) in 72% of cases.
  • Replicon: Col156 on 333 of 336. Median 5 CDS per plasmid.
  • 48% of the CDS on these plasmids are unannotatable. Two of the five or six genes on the canonical ColE1-like backbone have no name.
notebook zoom_two_dark_orfs.ipynb §2 — 87 distinct gene arrangements, modal one on 78 carriers

The fixed spacing is the strongest single piece of evidence on this slide. Random co-occurrence on a 5-gene plasmid would not produce ±2 on 87% of carriers, and it would not be never adjacent. The arrangement — one gene on each side of the relaxase — is what makes a mobilisation-accessory reading plausible.

Part 12 · The cassetteecology

Ecologically wide, genetically narrow — dissemination, not convergence

hosts

26 named species — mostly E. coli, with Klebsiella, Salmonella, Shigella, Enterobacter.

habitats

21 — human gut, blood, urine, wastewater, poultry.

countries

30, known for 226 of 336.

but lineages

4 MOB primary clusters, the largest holding 78%.

So the breadth is one backbone that has travelled, not many backbones converging on the same two genes. That distinction matters: it is a dissemination result, not a convergent-evolution result — and it is exactly the distinction the lineage control exists to make.

notebook zoom_two_dark_orfs.ipynb §3 · carrier table data/zoom_two_orfs/cassette_carriers.tsv

Two more facts that belong here. Zero AMR: none of the 336 carriers has a CARD hit — whatever these genes do, it is not resistance. And not a general mobile element: searched against the dark proteome of all 61,242 plasmids ≥20 kb, the pair hits 3 big plasmids between them, 0.005%. This is a small-plasmid feature.

Part 12 · The cassettewhat they might be

Almost invariant — and compositionally, a pair

Invariance

ORF-B is exactly 132 aa in all 365 copies; ORF-A exactly 177 aa in 98% of its 411. Within each family, 93% of proteins are exact duplicates of another member. Sequence that fixed across 30 countries and 21 habitats is under selection.

Composition

ORF-A: one hydrophobic segment above the transmembrane threshold (residues 104–112), net charge +2.
ORF-B: no hydrophobic window at all, net charge +6, 20% K/R.

The hypothesis

One membrane-associated protein and one basic soluble protein, flanking a relaxase. That is the arrangement of a mobilisation accessory module — and would also fit entry exclusion or a small regulatory system.

From amino-acid composition alone. Folding plus a structural search is the test that would settle it. Sequences are in data/zoom_two_orfs/two_reps.faa.

notebook zoom_two_dark_orfs.ipynb §4–§5caution hydropathy is a hypothesis generator, not a structure

Be explicit that no structure prediction has been run — amino-acid composition is the only structural read available and I am labelling it as such. If the room only takes one action item from this talk, it should be: fold these two and Foldseek them.

Part 12 · The cassettethe sting

ORF-A is a 20-protein family at 30% identity and a 400-plasmid family at 90%

thresholdrepresentativeproteinssubset of the looser family?
dark30GenBank_CP063716.1|620—
dark50GenBank_CP063716.1|620yes
dark70IMGPR_..._2609460067_000008|4494NO
dark90GenBank_CP063716.1|6411NO

The 494 proteins that form one family at 70% were split across two families at 30% — 482 in a 208 aa representative's cluster, 12 in ORF-A's.

Why the clusterings are not nested

-c 0.8 --cov-mode 0 requires 80% coverage of both sequences, so a 208 aa representative and a 155 aa protein can never share a family at any identity — 0.75 < 0.80.

At 30%, greedy set-cover makes the long protein a hub that absorbs everything it covers, stranding the short ones. At 70% the hub loses its long-range links and the short proteins coalesce.

A family being small at a loose threshold does not mean it is unimportant. The 30% view understated ORF-A twentyfold — and it would have been missed entirely by ranking families at that threshold, which is exactly how the 93-family shortlist was built.

notebook zoom_two_dark_orfs.ipynb §6

This generalises well beyond our dataset and it is the methodological finding I would most like feedback on. Any pipeline that picks a single identity threshold with symmetric coverage and then ranks families by size will systematically hide short proteins that sit near a longer hub. It is not a bug in MMseqs2 — it is the documented behaviour of greedy set-cover under a symmetric coverage constraint.

Part 13 · Where nextthe ledger

What we can claim, and what we cannot

Supported

  • The dark plasmidome is recurrent, not idiosyncratic — 84.4% of dark ORFs at 30%, still 70.3% at UniRef90.
  • The recurrence is not clonal redundancy — 63.9% of dark ORFs cross MOB lineage boundaries.
  • It is measurably part artifact: 28.5% is a PlasAnn annotation failure, and 18.5% of the whole dark proteome is machinery PlasAnn has a category for.
  • A genuine residue remains: 3,343 families, 115,811 ORFs, 30.6%, invisible to both tools.
  • Known anti-defense families do not explain it — 0.042%, from three independent directions.
  • “Payload-free” plasmids carry 3,647 defense systems, and our definition never excluded them.

Not established

  • No Pfam hit is not structural novelty. Profile HMMs stop well short of what structure comparison reaches.
  • Family boundaries are one defensible choice among several. The shortlist moves 93 → 5 across the sweep.
  • mob_cluster is a mash-based proxy, not a phylogeny, and the subset is lineage-skewed (AA379 holds 19,427 of 71,414).
  • PlasAnn's ORF calls are inherited, not verified — no independent gene calling was run.
  • The anti-defense negative rules out known families only — precisely the population the hypothesis predicts would be invisible.
  • Nothing here is expression evidence. We have not shown a single one of these proteins is made.
reports dark_orf_clustering.md · pfam_dark_validation.md · clustering_threshold_sensitivity.md · small_cryptic_methodology.md

Read the right-hand column at least as carefully as the left. The last bullet is the one that should bother us most: every claim in this deck is about sequence, and none of it is evidence that any of these ORFs is transcribed or translated.

Part 13 · Where nextnext, in order

Structure first — it is cheap, and it is the test we keep deferring

1 · Fold and search

ESMFold or AlphaFold over the 93 (and certainly the 5, and ORF-A/ORF-B), then Foldseek against AFDB + PDB + the ESM Atlas.

Structure reaches past profile HMMs. This converts “no Pfam hit at --cut_ga” into either a fold assignment or a real novelty claim. Median 130 aa — this is days, not months.

2 · Guilt by association

The PlasAnn shards carry CDS coordinates, and we have never used them for the dark set beyond the cassette. Acr genes are typically flanked by an HTH-containing aca gene; defense systems co-localise by definition.

A context scan is independent of homology — it can see what dbAPIS structurally cannot, which is exactly the gap our negative result leaves open.

3 · An orthogonal clustering

Every family boundary here comes from a sequence-identity threshold we had to pick. Protein language model embeddings (ESM-2 / ProtT5) plus a sequence-similarity network give a grouping with no identity knob, and would tell us which of our conclusions are about biology and which are about MMseqs2.

4 · Evidence that they are expressed

Nothing in this project shows these proteins are made. Human-gut and wastewater metatranscriptomes mapped to the carrier plasmids, or ribosome profiling where a matched dataset exists, would move the whole story from “conserved ORF” to “expressed protein”.

ready to go data/dark_orf_run/core_dark_families.tsv · recluster/core_dark_families_90.faa · data/zoom_two_orfs/two_reps.faa

Order matters here and it is an argument, not a list. Structure is first because it is the cheapest thing that can falsify our central claim. The context scan is second because it is the only proposal that attacks the anti-defense negative on its own terms. Embeddings are third because they are the honest answer to Part 6.

Part 13 · Where nextthe wet lab, and the edges

One experiment we could actually run, and four edges we have not touched

The tractable experiment

The cassette is the one object here that is ready for a bench. It sits on a Col156 ColE1-like mobilizable backbone in E. coli — a standard host, a small replicon, 336 sequenced carriers to pick a representative from.

  • Knock out ORF-A, ORF-B, and both; assay mobilisation frequency with a helper conjugative plasmid.
  • Test entry exclusion: does carriage reduce acquisition of a second Col plasmid?
  • Test stability over serial passage without selection.
  • Localise ORF-A — the composition predicts membrane association, and that is a one-experiment prediction.

Beyond <20 kb

The dark proteome of the 61,242 plasmids ≥20 kb appears in this project only as a negative control. It is the obvious next survey, and it would test whether “dark = small” is a real property or a size effect.

Beyond complete plasmids

We discarded 644,240 incomplete PlasmidScope entries. That is a defensible gate for a metadata study and a costly one for a family survey.

The plasmids with no genes at all

5,569 payload-free plasmids have no PlasAnn gene calls whatsoever and are absent from every analysis here. Independent gene calling would tell us whether that is a tool failure or a real property.

The phage–plasmid boundary

Small, ORF-dense, poorly typed replicons are exactly where phage-plasmids hide. We have not screened for them, and it is a plausible partial explanation for the residue.

candidate carriers data/zoom_two_orfs/cassette_carriers.tsv (336 rows, 30 countries)

Be honest that the wet-lab list is a proposal, not a plan — I have not costed it and I do not know who would run it. The ask is whether the group thinks it is worth a slot, and if so which of the four assays is the one that would actually change minds.

Part 13 · Where nextover to you

Five questions I would rather you answered than I guessed at

1 · Family definition

Is a sequence-identity threshold the right primitive at all, or should the whole survey be rebuilt on an SSN / embedding clustering with no knob to pick? Part 6 says our shortlist is mostly a property of the threshold.

2 · The lineage proxy

mob_cluster is mash-based and skewed — one cluster holds 19,427 of 71,414 plasmids. Is that good enough to carry the clonal-redundancy control, or do we need ANI dereplication or a real backbone phylogeny?

3 · Which candidate first

Of the five 90%-survivors and the cassette, which would you fold, synthesise, or knock out first — and does the cassette deserve a wet-lab slot at all?

4 · Expression data

Is there a published metatranscriptome over human-gut ColE1-like plasmids, or over Bacteroides cryptic plasmids, that we should be mining rather than generating?

5 · Is anti-defense dead?

Our negative rules out known families. Is a genomic-context scan worth the effort, or is the honest read that plasmid anti-defense is already annotated and the dark fraction is something else entirely?

And the uncomfortable one

Is 57.4% a discovery or a measurement of how bad plasmid annotation is? We think it is both. We would like to know where this room draws that line.

everything is reproducible notebooks_my/*.ipynb read finished outputs; no notebook re-runs a search

Stop here and let the room talk. If discussion stalls, question 3 is the one that always restarts it — people have opinions about which protein they would fold.
